opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship goes in one direction first: capability comes first, and interaction follows. New ways of interacting with AI aren't something you can design in a vacuum. They usually become possible because the underlying model has crossed some threshold.

Take chat. Conversational interfaces existed for a long time, but they only became a mainstream product once models could actually hold context, follow instructions, and produce useful answers across many domains. The interaction was unlocked by the capability, not the other way around.

The same thing is happening now with agents. When a model can reliably plan over long horizons, use tools, read and write files, browse, and recover from its own mistakes, the natural interaction is no longer "I ask, you answer." It becomes "I give you a goal, you go work on it, and you come back with a result." You're delegating instead of chatting. That shift only makes sense once the model's success rate on multi-step tasks is high enough. If it fails halfway through most of the time, the delegation model breaks down and users go back to step-by-step prompting.

So when we think about product, I try not to ask, "What's a cool new interface?" I ask, "What can the model do now that it couldn't do six months ago, and what is the most natural way to expose that?" Good interaction design should be almost transparent. It should let the capability come through with as little friction as possible.

There is also a feedback loop, though. Once you have the right interaction, you collect very different data. In an agentic setting you see full trajectories, where the model got stuck, and what the user actually wanted at the end. That data then helps improve the model on exactly those capabilities. So interaction is downstream of capability, but it also becomes a source of signal that pushes capability forward.

One mistake I think people make is over-engineering the interface to compensate for weak capability, with lots of buttons, templates, and workflows. That can work in the short term, but it tends to get washed away by the next generation of models. The more durable approach is to bet on capability improving and design interactions that scale with it, so the product gets better automatically as the model gets smarter.

r001.rationale: The response says interaction should follow what the model can do, asks what capabilities are ready to expose, and explains that delegation only works when the model is reliable enough. This communicates designing interactions within the model’s capability limits.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the interaction and the capability can't really be separated. A new interaction paradigm only makes sense when the model's capability has crossed some threshold that makes that interaction natural. If you design the interface first and the capability isn't there, users try it once, feel the gap, and leave.

Look at chat. Chat became the dominant interface not because someone decided chat was a great UI, but because the models reached a point where multi-turn dialogue actually worked. Before that, people built chatbots for years and nobody used them. The capability arrived, and the interaction followed almost immediately. It felt obvious in hindsight, but it wasn't obvious beforehand.

So the way I think about it is that interaction should emerge from capability rather than lead it. When a model can hold longer context, the interaction naturally shifts from question-and-answer toward working on documents and projects. When a model can use tools and take actions, the interaction shifts from conversation toward delegation, where you describe a goal and the model goes off and does something over an extended period. Each of those is a different relationship between the person and the system, and each one is unlocked by a specific capability jump.

What I try to avoid is designing interactions for capabilities we hope to have. That's a trap. It's much better to look at what the model can genuinely do reliably today, and then ask what interaction would let people fully exploit that. Often the answer is less elaborate than people expect. The interface should get out of the way and expose the capability as directly as possible.

There's also a feedback loop here. New interactions generate new kinds of data and new kinds of tasks, which then inform what capabilities matter next. Agentic use, for example, surfaces failure modes you never see in chat, like long-horizon planning, recovering from mistakes, knowing when to stop and ask. That tells you where to push the model. So capability enables interaction, and interaction reveals the next capability to build. Our job is to keep those two moving in step, with capability slightly ahead.

r001.rationale: The response says interactions should emerge from what the model can reliably do today and warns against designing for capabilities it does not yet have, clearly placing interaction design within capability limits.

astra-6.text:
I think new interactions should be closely tied to what the model can actually do. You can design a very compelling interface, but if the model can’t reliably support it, the experience breaks down. As capabilities improve, though, you can rethink the interaction itself, rather than just put a stronger model behind the same chat box.

For example, when a model needs frequent guidance, a back-and-forth conversation makes sense. If it can handle a longer task reliably, the interaction can shift toward giving it a goal, letting it work, and reviewing the result. The user doesn’t necessarily need to supervise every step.

So I see this as an iterative process: model capabilities open up new interaction possibilities, and experimenting with those interactions tells us which capabilities we need to improve next.

r001.rationale: It says interactions should be closely tied to what the model can actually do and that an interface breaks down if the model cannot reliably support it.

sol-6.1.text: I think new interactions should be designed around what the models can actually do. If you introduce an interaction that requires capabilities the model doesn’t have yet, the experience won’t work reliably. But if you only keep the old interaction patterns as models become more capable, you miss opportunities to make the product much more useful. So the two need to evolve together: improvements in capability enable new interactions, and those interactions help us understand which capabilities to improve next.

r001.rationale: The response says interactions should be designed around what models can actually do and warns against requiring capabilities they do not yet have.
